summary: Summarizes perceived problems in the structure, function and processes of the IETF, digested from mailing-list discussion between November 2002 and September 2003. It tries to find root causes to guide later process improvement. It is informational.

eli5.summary: People who make internet rules listed what annoyed them about how the group works, so they could fix it.

questions: what is wrong with the ietf process
what problems did the ietf identify in its processes
why is the ietf hard to manage
what is the ietf mission problem
subtitle: An analysis of problems in IETF structure and processes from the community's own feedback.

tldr.problem: By the early 2000s, the IETF had grown from a small focused group to a much larger organization, but its management structure and processes had not adapted to its new size, leading to inefficiency, slow decision-making, and frustration among participants.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC identifies root causes of the problems from extensive community discussion: unclear mission, weak engineering practices, poor handling of complex standards, overworked management, and inadequate engagement from participants.
tldr.outcome: The analysis provides a foundation for IETF process reform. By naming the structural problems rather than blaming individuals, the IETF can redesign its processes to match its current scale and complexity.

facts.label: Document readership
facts.value: 5% or less of working group attendees read drafts

today: RFC 3774 is informational and reflects problems identified in 2002–2003. The IETF has made changes since then, including reforms to working group structure, better documentation, and more formalized processes, though ongoing challenges around scale and engagement persist.

sections.title: The IETF's Growth and Challenges
sections.content:
The Internet Engineering Task Force started as a small, focused group of engineers working on a clearly defined mission. Between 1989 and 1999, the IETF grew by a factor of ten or more in both participants and workload. The scope of the IETF also expanded dramatically as the internet became more complex and touched more areas of life.

This RFC summarizes problems that the IETF community identified during discussions between late 2002 and mid-2003. The document does not aim to blame individuals but to recognize structural problems—the kinds that arise when an organization fails to adapt its management structure and processes as it grows. The raw material comes from mailing list discussions and prior drafts analyzing IETF challenges.
sections.eli5: The group that creates internet standards grew from a handful of people to thousands. The problems people complained about are not anyone's fault—they're just what happens when a small-team way of working gets stretched to a much bigger group.

sections.title: The Root Cause Approach
sections.content:
Rather than listing every perceived problem, the RFC identifies underlying root causes. Many problems are symptoms of a few core issues. For example, slow document approval might stem from weak charter clarity (an engineering practice problem), overworked area directors (a management structure problem), or lack of clear IETF mission (a strategic problem). By fixing root causes, many symptoms should improve together.

The document does not rank the root causes by importance; instead, it notes they are interlinked. The roots identified are: lack of common mission understanding, weak engineering practices, difficulty with large and complex standards, poor use of the maturity levels, workload exceeding engaged participants, mismatched management structure, working group dynamics issues, and inadequately prepared leaders.
sections.eli5: Instead of making a huge list of complaints, the RFC looks for the main problems underneath. Fix the root, and the branches should improve on their own.

sections.title: Mission, Scope, and Engagement
sections.content:
The IETF lacks a clearly stated, widely understood mission. It is unsure what it should work on, who its stakeholders are, and what impact it should have in the market. Without a clear mission, working groups lack clear charters, and individual RFCs lack clear purposes. This affects everything from deciding if a proposed standard is in-scope to creating the roadmaps stakeholders need to understand the IETF's direction.

Additionally, the IETF's workload has grown faster than its engaged participant base. Although meetings have large attendance, only a small fraction of attendees read documents under discussion. Volunteers frequently miss deadlines for writing and reviewing work. Beyond RFC authorship and a few formal leadership roles, the IETF offers little formal recognition for contributions, which can lead motivated people to leave because they cannot obtain recognition to fuel their enthusiasm or justify IETF attendance to their employers.
sections.eli5: The IETF doesn't clearly say what it's trying to do, so working groups don't know what they're supposed to build. There's also more work than people have time for, and most volunteers don't get recognized for helping out.

sections.title: Leadership Workload and Scope of Authority
sections.content:
The IETF's management structure has remained largely unchanged since 1992, even as the organization has more than tripled in size and complexity. Authority is concentrated in the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG), particularly its Area Directors (ADs), who serve as senior managers for working groups and quality gatekeepers for all IETF documents.

The workload of each AD is enormous: they must understand their technical area in detail and all related work, read and form opinions on hundreds of documents, interact with working group chairs and participants, coordinate across other areas, and often manage junior directors—all as a part-time role. The result is overwork, slow decision-making, and difficulty in recruiting new leaders who can commit the required time.

The concentrated authority also means a small group has disproportionate influence. The IESG's discretionary power, while designed to allow flexibility, is not always exercised fairly or transparently. Appeal mechanisms are weak, and the only sanction—recall—is seen as excessive for most offenses, making ADs feel unaccountable.
sections.eli5: A small group of ADs has almost all the decision-making power, but there's so much work that they can't keep up. When they're overloaded, standards get stuck. New leaders don't want the job because it's too much work on the side.

sections.title: Standards Development Process and Quality
sections.content:
The IETF's standards development process lacks consistent, rigorous engineering practices. Working groups do not reliably produce timely, high-quality, predictable output. Contributing problems include failure to establish clear scope at the start, poor identification of issues before design is frozen, and continued refinement beyond what the requirements demand.

The three-level maturity hierarchy (Proposed, Draft, and Full Standard) is not being used as intended. Most standards remain at Proposed Standard level forever. The original intent was for standards to mature through implementation and deployment experience, but implementation is not required, so the 'rough consensus and running code' principle does not work as designed. Additionally, there is no formal bug reporting or tracking system for IETF RFCs, and periodic reviews of lower-level standards are not performed.

Project management techniques are rarely applied to IETF work. Charters often lack fine-grained milestones, detailed timelines are missing, and estimated completion times often differ widely from actual ones. The IETF also has difficulty with large and complex standards that require engineering across multiple areas; its structure emphasizes vertical communication through area directors rather than horizontal coordination between working groups.
sections.eli5: Standards take a long time because there's no clear plan, no tracking of bugs, and not enough testing with real code. Big, complicated standards are especially hard because different teams don't coordinate well with each other.

sections.title: Working Groups, Relationships, and Preparation
sections.content:
Working group dynamics can make it hard to reach closure on issues. Some working groups are hijacked by sectional interests. Participants from outside the 'affinity group' of experienced leaders—who tend to share a North American, English-speaking cultural background—find it harder to be heard, especially if English is not their native language. This concentrates influence among a small group and makes newer or international participants feel excluded.

The IETF also relies heavily on personal relationships: decisions are made among people who have worked together for years, and informal communication channels matter more than formal ones. This can exclude newcomers and reduce transparency.

Finally, IETF participants and leaders are often inadequately prepared for their roles. Working group chairs, area directors, and other leaders receive little training or guidance. The IETF assumes competence but does not invest in developing skills or transferring knowledge from experienced leaders to newcomers.
sections.eli5: Working groups can get stuck or hijacked. The same people end up making decisions because they've worked together for years. New people and international people have a harder time being heard. And nobody really trains people for their jobs.

items.title: Unclear Mission
items.text: IETF lacks a clearly defined, commonly understood mission, scope, and stakeholder focus.

items.title: Weak Engineering
items.text: Inconsistent engineering practices, poor quality gates, and lack of rigorous project management.

items.title: Complexity
items.text: Difficulty handling large, complex standards that cross multiple technical areas.

items.title: Overloaded Leadership
items.text: Management structure not scaled to organization size; ADs carry unsustainable workload.

items.title: Low Engagement
items.text: Workload exceeds engaged participants; many members participate passively or not at all.

items.title: Process Ossification
items.text: Procedures are becoming rigid rules rather than flexible guidelines with IESG discretion.
